extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of social philosophy/sociology and historians of political society
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for forming reliable generalizations about society from historical evidence, specifying methodological principles (statics vs dynamics), necessary verifications, and the requisites of stable political societies. Intended to direct how to derive scientific sociological laws from history and human-nature principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressiveness assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a progressive change both in the character of the human race and in their outward circumstances—that in each successive age the principal phenomena of society are different from what they were in the age preceding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat human societies as changing across generations (not merely day-to-day); use generation-length intervals as the primary units for historical comparison. Do not confuse 'progressive' with 'improvement' — progressiveness is a methodological premise about change, not necessarily moral or material improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical historical generalizations require connection to laws of human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Any generalization from history can only be an empirical law until it is connected with the psychological and ethological laws which govern the action of circumstances on men and of men on circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept an empirical sequence from history as a scientific law unless you can deduce it from, or at least show its consilience with, underlying laws of human nature; otherwise it is unreliable for predicting beyond adjacent cases. M. Comte's approach is noted as recognizing this necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never introduce historical generalizations without sufficient grounds in human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an imperative rule never to introduce any generalization from history into the social science unless sufficient grounds can be pointed out for it in human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require either a priori justificatory reasons grounded in human nature or repeated verification by laws of psychology/ethology before using historical generalizations in social-theoretical claims. Treat purely empirical regularities as provisional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constant verification of empirical laws by psychological and ethological laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The only check or corrective on erroneous generalizations from history is constant verification by psychological and ethological laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subject historical inferences to ongoing cross-checks with knowledge about human nature; use expert competence in psychology/ethology to evaluate which historical facts matter and how they should be interpreted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence requirement for those preparing historical generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: No one but a person competently skilled in those [psychological and ethological] laws is capable of preparing the materials for historical generalization, by analyzing the facts of history, or even by observing the social phenomena of his own time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection and weighting of historical evidence requires specialized knowledge; non-experts may fail to identify comparatively important facts or to infer unseen facts correctly. Prefer reviewers/authors with demonstrable competence in human-nature laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Social Statics and Social Dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: The Empirical Laws of Society are of two kinds; some are uniformities of co-existence, some of succession. According as the science is occupied in ascertaining and verifying the former sort of uniformities or the latter, M. Comte gives it the title of Social Statics, or of Social Dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing social phenomena, be explicit whether you are studying conditions of equilibrium (statics/coexistence) or laws of progress (dynamics/succession). Use the appropriate conceptual tools for each branch and avoid conflating simultaneity with sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine statical and dynamical views to discover laws of correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary to combine the statical view of social phenomena with the dynamical, considering not only the progressive changes of the different elements, but the contemporaneous condition of each; and thus obtain empirically the law of correspondence not only between the simultaneous states, but between the simultaneous changes, of those elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical laws improve when you study how elements co-exist and how their changes correlate across time. Seek correspondences between contemporaneous states and between contemporaneous rates/directions of change to infer derivative laws of development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use an element predominant in social movement as a central chain
rubrics_metrics.description: If some one element in the complex existence of social man is pre-eminent as the prime agent of the social movement, we could take the progress of that one element as the central chain... the succession of the facts would thus present a more spontaneous order approaching real filiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and prioritize the social element that most strongly drives change (historically, Mill argues, the 'state of the speculative faculties' or prevailing beliefs). Use that element as the organizing axis to relate other elements' progressions when reconstructing social filiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of speculative faculties (state of knowledge) in social progress
rubrics_metrics.description: There really is one social element which is thus predominant... This is, the state of the speculative faculties of mankind; including the nature of the beliefs which by any means they have arrived at concerning themselves and the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining or predicting large social transformations, foreground changes in knowledge, belief systems, and intellectual convictions as proximate causes. Historical precedents show intellectual change commonly precedes large material or institutional shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overreliance on few instances and acknowledge empirical-law limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The empirical laws must be the result of but a few instances, since few nations have ever attained... If one or two of these few instances be insufficiently known... nothing is more probable than that a wrong empirical law will emerge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about generalizing from limited or badly analyzed cases; demand adequate comparative data and explicit statements of scope and limits. Use psychological/ethological consistency as a corrective to small-sample overgeneralization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect inference among social elements (analogy to anatomy) with caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Each social element should be always and exclusively considered relatively to all the other elements, with the whole of which it is united by mutual interdependence... the provisions of sociology will enable us to infer one from another (subject to ulterior verification by direct observation) the various characteristic marks of each distinct mode of social existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is legitimate to infer the condition of one social element from the known condition of related elements, especially when direct observation is impracticable; however, be explicit about the assumptions, avoid oversimple causal mappings, and estimate limits of variation to prevent error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisites of a State: laws, tribunals, and organized executive force
rubrics_metrics.description: No numerous society has ever been held together without laws, or usages equivalent to them; without tribunals, and an organized force of some sort to execute their decisions. There have always been public authorities whom... the rest of the community obeyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether a collective entity qualifies as a State, look for the existence of legal/usage rules, adjudicative bodies, and an enforcement mechanism (organized force); absence of these indicates lack of collective independent existence or the need to reclassify the social form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisite of education with restraining discipline for political stability
rubrics_metrics.description: There has existed... a system of education, beginning with infancy and continued through life, of which one main and incessant ingredient was restraining discipline... to train the human being in the habit... of subordinating his personal impulses and aims to what were considered the ends of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess political stability in part by the presence and rigor of socializing institutions that inculcate obedience and self-restraint. Relaxation of such discipline correlates with internal disorganization and susceptibility to decline or despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisite of allegiance/loyalty as a fixed point
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be... the existence, in some form or other, of the feeling of allegiance or loyalty... that there be in the constitution of the state something which is settled, something permanent, and not to be called in question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a polity contains a widely accepted 'fixed point'—a sacred or unquestioned element (gods, persons, laws, principles)—that anchors loyalty. Chronic contestation of such fundamentals indicates a state effectively in civil war and unlikely to maintain long-term cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisite of social cohesion (sympathy, common interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong and active principle of cohesion among the members of the same community or state... a feeling of common interest... that one part of the community do not consider themselves as foreigners with regard to another part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure cohesion by the degree to which people identify as one people and share concern for each other's welfare (not xenophobic nationalism). Weak internal cohesion predicts fragmentation, secessionist tendencies, or vulnerability to external domination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider international reciprocal influences and degree of consensus across nations
rubrics_metrics.description: The evolution of each people... is gradually brought under the influence... of the other nations of the earth... in different contemporaneous nations the perpetual reciprocity of influence... the consensus must... decrease with the affinity of the cases and the multiplicity of the points of contact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In comparative historical work, account for cross-national influences and diffusion; expect greater convergence among culturally/temporally proximate societies and near independence among distant ones (e.g., Western Europe vs Eastern Asia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of a priori prediction due to cumulative interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: So long a series of actions and reactions between Circumstances and Man... could not possibly be computed by human faculties from the elementary laws which produce it. The mere length of the series would be a sufficient obstacle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the practical impossibility of deriving long-run historical sequences purely a priori from elementary human laws because minor errors compound; therefore emphasize empirical verification and caution in long-term forecasting.
